title: 3D Printing: Building Layer by Layer
summary: How a 3D printer turns a computer design into a solid object by adding thin layers of melted material, and how doctors, inventors, builders, and astronauts use it.
poll: Every school should have a 3D printer.

versions.title: A Printer That Makes Things
versions.text:
Most printers put ink on a page. Not this one! A 3D printer makes real things. You can hold them. It can make a toy. It can make a cup or a tool.

First, a person makes a plan. The plan is on a computer. This plan is the design. It shows the shape.

Then the printer gets to work. It has a hot tip. A long string of plastic goes in. The heat makes the plastic melt. Soft plastic comes out of the tip.

The tip moves back and forth. It lays down one thin, flat sheet. This sheet is a layer. Then it lays a new layer on top. Then one more. Each layer cools. It gets hard.

Step by step, the thing grows. It can take hours. At last, it is done!

The old way was to cut a big block. A lot of it got thrown out. A 3D printer just uses what it needs.

Doctors use 3D printers. They make hands and arms for kids. Some builders print the walls of a house!

Step by step, the thing grows. It can take hours. But at the end, it is done!

The old way was to cut a big block. A lot was thrown out. A 3D printer uses just what it needs.

Doctors use 3D printers. They make hands and arms for kids who need them. Some builders even print the walls of a house!

versions.title: Building Layer by Layer
versions.text:
Most printers put ink on paper. A 3D printer is very different. It makes real things that you can hold in your hand. It can make a toy, a cup, a phone case, or a tool.

First, a person makes a plan on a computer. This plan is called the design. It shows the exact shape of the thing.

Next, the printer gets to work. Inside it is a hot tip. A long string of plastic feeds into the tip. The heat makes the plastic melt. Then the soft plastic squeezes out.

The tip moves back and forth. It draws one thin, flat sheet. This sheet is called a layer. Then the printer adds a new layer on top. Then it adds one more. Each layer cools and turns hard.

Layer by layer, the object grows taller. A small toy may take an hour. A big thing can take a whole day.

The old way was to cut a shape out of a big block. A lot of the block was thrown away. A 3D printer uses only what it needs, so there is less waste.

Many people use 3D printers. Doctors print hands and arms for kids who need them. Some builders even print the walls of a house!

versions.title: 3D Printing: Building Layer by Layer
versions.text:
Most printers spread ink across a sheet of paper. A 3D printer does something very different. It creates solid objects that you can pick up and hold. It can make toys, cups, phone cases, and even tools.

Every object begins as a plan on a computer. This plan is called the design. It shows the exact shape and size of the object. Then a computer program slices the design into hundreds of very thin pieces.

Next, the printer gets to work. Many printers use a long string of plastic that is wound on a roll. The plastic feeds into a hot tip. The heat makes the plastic melt, and the soft plastic squeezes out like toothpaste from a tube.

The tip moves back and forth to draw one thin, flat sheet. This sheet is called a layer. When the first layer is finished, the printer adds another layer on top. Each layer cools quickly and becomes hard, so it can hold up the next one.

Layer by layer, the object grows taller. A small toy may take about an hour. A large object can take a whole day or more.

In the past, people often made things by cutting a shape out of a big block of wood or metal. Much of the block ended up as waste. A 3D printer adds only the plastic it needs, so less is thrown away.

Today, 3D printers help in many places. Doctors print hands and arms for children who need them. Dentists print teeth. Builders in some countries, including Saudi Arabia, have even printed the walls of houses!

versions.title: 3D Printing: Building Layer by Layer
versions.text:
Most printers spread ink across a flat sheet of paper, but a 3D printer accomplishes something remarkably different. It produces solid objects that you can pick up and examine, including toys, cups, phone cases, and practical tools.

Every object begins as a design on a computer. The design is a digital model that records the exact shape and measurements of the object. A special program then slices the model into hundreds of extremely thin pieces, which tells the printer precisely what to construct at each stage.

Many home printers use a long thread of plastic that is wound around a spool. The plastic is pushed into a nozzle, a small metal tip that becomes extremely hot. The heat causes the plastic to melt, and the softened material squeezes out like toothpaste from a tube.

The nozzle travels back and forth to draw one thin, flat layer. When the first layer is complete, the printer deposits another layer on top of it. Each layer cools rapidly and hardens, so it can support the next one. Gradually, the object rises higher. A small toy might take an hour, while a large object can require a day or longer.

Traditionally, manufacturers created products by cutting a shape out of a large block of wood or metal, and much of the material became waste. A 3D printer adds only the material it requires, so considerably less is discarded.

3D printers are also valuable for testing inventions. An engineer can print a prototype, which is an early model, and determine whether it functions properly before producing many copies. If a problem appears, the engineer can modify the design and print again within hours.

Today, 3D printers assist people in numerous fields. Doctors print custom hands and arms that fit a particular child perfectly, and dentists print replacement teeth. Some printers use metal or concrete instead of plastic, and builders in several countries, including Saudi Arabia, have printed the walls of entire houses. Astronauts on the International Space Station have even printed tools in orbit.

versions.title: 3D Printing: Building Layer by Layer
versions.text:
Most printers spread ink across a flat sheet of paper, but a 3D printer accomplishes something remarkably different: it manufactures solid objects that people can hold, examine, and use, ranging from toys and phone cases to practical household tools.

Every object originates as a design on a computer. The design is a digital model that records the precise shape and measurements of the object, and specialized software then slices this model into hundreds of extremely thin horizontal pieces, which instructs the printer exactly what to construct at each stage.

Many home printers use filament, a long thread of plastic wound around a spool. The filament is pushed into a nozzle, a small metal tip heated to a high temperature, and the heat causes the plastic to melt. The softened material then emerges in a narrow stream, much like toothpaste squeezed from a tube.

The nozzle travels back and forth to trace one thin, flat layer. When the first layer is complete, the printer deposits another layer on top, and each layer cools rapidly and hardens so that it can support the next. Depending on its size, an object might require an hour or more than a day to finish.

Engineers call this process additive manufacturing, because the machine adds material rather than removing it. Traditionally, factories created products by cutting a shape out of a solid block of wood or metal, a method that generated considerable waste. A 3D printer uses only the material it requires, so significantly less is discarded.

The first 3D printer was invented during the 1980s by an American engineer named Chuck Hull, whose machine used a beam of ultraviolet light to harden a liquid, one layer at a time. Today, some printers still use light, while others use powerful lasers to fuse metal powder.

These machines now assist people in numerous fields. Inventors print prototypes to test ideas quickly, and doctors print prosthetic hands that fit a particular child perfectly. Dentists print replacement teeth, and builders in several countries, including Saudi Arabia, have printed the concrete walls of houses. Astronauts aboard the International Space Station have even printed tools in orbit. However, when a company needs millions of identical items, traditional factory methods are usually still faster and cheaper.

keyWords.definition: a machine that makes copies, or that builds things from a plan on a computer
keyWords.example: The printer in our classroom ran out of paper.

keyWords.definition: one thin, flat sheet of something that lies on top of or under another
keyWords.example: My grandmother's cake has a layer of cream in the middle.

keyWords.definition: a light, strong material made by people that can be shaped when it is hot
keyWords.example: The bottle is made of clear plastic.

keyWords.definition: a plan or drawing that shows how something will look and be made
keyWords.example: Sara drew a design for a new park with lots of shade.

keyWords.definition: to turn from a hard solid into a soft or runny form because of heat
keyWords.example: The chocolate began to melt in the hot car.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How a 3D printer builds things one layer at a time
How to fix a paper printer when it runs out of ink
Why plastic is bad for the sea
How doctors learn their jobs at a big school
questions.why: The article explains how a 3D printer turns a design into a real object by adding layers, and how people use it.

wrong.B: The article does not talk about fixing printers or ink.
wrong.C: The article does not discuss plastic in the sea.
wrong.D: Doctors are mentioned only as people who use 3D printers.

questions.stem: What goes into the hot tip of the printer?
options: A sheet of paper
Some wet ink in many bright colors
A long string of plastic
A small block of wood
questions.why: The article says a long string of plastic goes into the hot tip.

wrong.A: Paper is used by normal printers, not this one.
wrong.B: A 3D printer does not use ink in the article.
wrong.D: Wood blocks belong to the old way of cutting shapes.

questions.stem: What do doctors make with 3D printers?
options: Beds for a hospital
Pills for sick people
Glasses for people who cannot see well
Hands and arms for kids who need them
questions.why: The article says doctors use 3D printers to make hands and arms for kids.

questions.stem: The tip lays down one thin, flat sheet called a layer. What is a layer?
options: A hot tool for cutting
One thin sheet that lies on top of another
A kind of computer game that kids can play
A string of soft plastic
questions.why: The article explains that a layer is one thin, flat sheet, and new layers go on top.

wrong.C: A layer has nothing to do with games.
wrong.D: The string of plastic goes into the tip; a layer is what comes out flat.

questions.stem: What happens FIRST when a 3D printer makes something?
options: A person makes a design on a computer.
The plastic cools and gets hard.
The tip lays down the top layer.
The thing is done and ready to use.
questions.why: The article says first a person makes a plan, or design, on a computer.

wrong.B: Cooling comes after each layer is laid down.
wrong.C: The top layer comes near the end.
wrong.D: Being done is the last step.

questions.stem: Why is the plastic soft when it comes out of the tip?
options: It is mixed with water.
It is very old plastic.
The heat makes it melt.
The tip squeezes it very hard.
questions.why: The tip is hot, and the heat makes the plastic melt, so it comes out soft.

wrong.B: The age of the plastic is not mentioned.
wrong.D: The plastic gets soft from heat, not from squeezing.

questions.stem: Why might a 3D printer be better than cutting a shape from a big block?
options: It is always much faster.
Less of the plastic gets thrown out.
It never needs a plan.
It works without any power at all, even at night.
questions.why: When you cut a block, a lot is thrown out; a 3D printer uses just what it needs.

wrong.A: The article says printing can take hours, so it is not always faster.
wrong.C: Every print starts with a design.
wrong.D: A hot tip needs power to heat up.

questions.stem: Why does the author first say that most printers put ink on a page?
options: To teach how to buy ink
To tell readers to print their homework
To prove that paper is strong
To show how a 3D printer is different
questions.why: Starting with a normal printer helps readers see how different a 3D printer is, since it makes real things.

wrong.A: The article does not talk about buying ink.
wrong.C: The strength of paper is not discussed.

LOW.prompt: If you had a 3D printer, what would you make? Explain how the printer would build it, using two facts from the article.
checklist: I used at least two facts from the article.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: If I had a 3D printer, I would make a toy for my little brother. The printer would start from a design on the computer and melt plastic to squeeze it out like toothpaste. Layer by layer, the plastic would build up until my toy was finished.

MID.prompt: Explain how a 3D printer turns a design into a solid object. Use at least three steps from the article in the correct order.

I used at least three details from the article.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
MID.modelAnswer: First, a design is made on a computer, and a program slices it into hundreds of thin layers. Then, the nozzle melts plastic material and squeezes it out to draw the first flat layer, which cools and hardens quickly. Finally, the printer adds layer after layer on top until the whole custom object is complete, using only the material it needs so little is wasted.

HIGH.prompt: The author says 3D printing creates less waste but is not always the best choice. Explain both sides using evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained one advantage and one limit of 3D printing.
I used evidence from the article for each point.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
HIGH.modelAnswer: One advantage of 3D printing is that it wastes very little material, because this additive process only adds the plastic filament a design actually needs, unlike cutting a shape out of a big block where much of the material is thrown away. Doctors and dentists also use this precise process to manufacture custom prosthetic hands and teeth that fit one person perfectly. However, 3D printing is not always the best choice, since a small toy might take an hour to print while a large object can take a day or more, which makes it too slow for producing many identical copies quickly.
